gloss_distractors: a habit of avoiding hard decisions
senses.definition: Coming across as calm, clear and senior enough to be handed a decision.
senses.caution: Only say it about other people. As feedback it is vague, so add a specific behaviour, such as leading with your recommendation.
senses.example: Her content is watertight; what we are coaching is executive presence, starting with not burying the ask on slide nine.

cues.text: A brilliant engineer keeps losing the room in front of the investment committee, and you need the two-word term leadership coaches use for what he has to build.
Your manager asks what separates two candidates for a director role with identical track records, and the answer is that only one of them looks and sounds ready to be handed the decision.
You are designing a coaching plan for someone who knows more than anyone in the room but is never the one the MD turns to.
A friend preparing for a panel interview for a senior role asks what the panel is judging when it watches how calm, clear and senior she seems in the first two minutes.

distractors: A record of delivering what you promised, quarter after quarter.
The number of people who report to you, directly and indirectly.
The ability to speak a second language well enough to negotiate in it.
The set of decisions a leader is formally allowed to make without asking.
The rank a job sits at in a company's grading system, published for everyone to see.

gloss_distractors: a willingness to take large risks
senses.definition: Skill in handling something delicate so smoothly that the difficulty never shows.
senses.caution: As a verb it can suggest you hid a problem instead of solving it. Do not use it about numbers or facts, especially with auditors or in writing.
senses.example: He finessed the headcount question without promising anything, and the MD moved on.

cues.text: A colleague deflects a budget question without either lying or conceding ground, and you want the word for how deftly it was done.
You are describing how a tense vendor negotiation was closed with nobody losing face.
A friend steered her parents off a touchy subject at dinner with no argument at all.
A footballer beats a defender with one soft touch instead of pace, and you want the word for that kind of skill.

distractors: Brute force applied until an obstacle gives way.
Doing a job to a standard nobody asked for, at a cost nobody agreed to.
A rehearsed answer prepared in advance for a question you expect to be asked.
The willingness to say the uncomfortable thing in a room that does not want to hear it.
The care taken to record exactly how a decision was reached, so it can be audited later.
